claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical integrity of near-equiatomic multicomponent nanoparticles is governed by the extent and nature of short-range chemical ordering.
Short-range chemical ordering creates local energy barriers that inhibit rapid atomic diffusion.
Short-range chemical ordering suppresses phase segregation, elemental rearrangement, and high-temperature sintering.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, near-equiatomic, single-phase HEA solid solutions.
The initial HEA nanoparticles are produced by a solution-based colloidal or solvothermal synthesis.
The initial particles exhibit high configurational entropy.
The initial particles have a random distribution of constituent elements and no short-range order.
Annealing at approximately 600 K under an inert or reducing atmosphere will produce moderate short-range order without triggering full phase segregation.
Short-range order consists of energetically favorable local atomic motifs.
Development of short-range order reduces local lattice disorder.
Reduced atomic diffusivity can contribute to thermal stability in HEAs.
Annealed nanoparticles with enhanced short-range order will exhibit less sintering than untreated nanoparticles during high-temperature service.
Annealed nanoparticles with enhanced short-range order will exhibit less phase segregation than untreated nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles will retain catalytic performance better than untreated nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles will retain thermoelectric performance better than untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equiatomic, single-phase HEA nanoparticles operating at high temperature in inert or reducing atmospheres.
Applicability to strongly oxidizing environments and to non-equiatomic or multiphase systems is undetermined.
Excessive ordering may reduce catalytic activity by impeding or removing active sites.
